title: Rahul Roy Opens Up About Speech Recovery Six Years After Brain Stroke
excerpt: The Aashiqui actor says he takes eight medicines daily and has switched to a vegan diet since suffering a cerebrovascular stroke in 2020.
body:
• Actor Rahul Roy has spoken about his ongoing recovery from a 2020 brain stroke that left him unable to walk or talk
  • He takes eight medicines daily and has switched to a strict vegan and Jain diet, giving up smoking, meat, onion, garlic and dairy
  • Roy is returning to acting with the series Super Badshah on Kuku TV alongside Karanvir Bohra
  • A neurologist notes that post-stroke recovery requires a balanced, nutrient-rich diet and consistent medical management

Actor Rahul Roy, who became a household name with the 1990 romantic musical Aashiqui, has spoken candidly about the difficult road to recovery after suffering a brain stroke six years ago, revealing that he still takes eight medicines every day and was uncertain whether he would ever walk or talk again.

The Stroke and Its Aftermath

Roy suffered a cerebrovascular stroke in November 2020 while filming LAC – Live the Battle in Kargil. He was rushed to Srinagar and later transferred to Nanavati Hospital in Mumbai, where he spent time in the ICU. The initial phase of his recovery was marked by profound uncertainty.

"After my brain stroke, I didn't even know if I would be able to walk or talk again. I used to be a heavy smoker and a non-vegetarian, but I've turned vegan."

— Rahul Roy, in an interview with Free Press Journal

His speech difficulties remained a concern for years after the stroke. "The only thing I was sceptical about was my speech problem because of the brain stroke," he told the Free Press Journal, adding that his co-star Karanvir Bohra was supportive throughout the process of returning to acting.

A Complete Lifestyle Overhaul

The health crisis prompted Roy to make sweeping changes to his daily life. The actor, who was previously a heavy smoker and non-vegetarian, has adopted a strict vegan and Jain diet, avoiding onion, garlic and dairy products. His mornings now begin with a rigid medication routine.

"Every day after breakfast, I have 8 medicines. But things are much better now than before," he said, reflecting on how far he has come since the medical emergency.

Dr. Yogesh Godge, a consultant neurologist at Jupiter Hospital in Thane, noted that while no single diet can reverse brain damage caused by a stroke, a balanced, nutrient-rich diet can support overall recovery and cardiovascular health. The focus, he said, should be on controlling risk factors that could trigger another stroke.

Return to the Screen

Roy's last major screen appearance was in filmmaker Kanu Behl's psychological drama Agra, which released in Indian theatres in November 2025. He is now preparing for a comeback with Kuku TV's upcoming series Super Badshah, in which he plays an underworld don opposite Karanvir Bohra.

The Bigg Boss Season 1 winner has maintained that continuing to work remains essential for both his financial independence and emotional recovery, even as he manages the lingering effects of the stroke.

A Broader Message

Roy's story resonates beyond celebrity news. Stroke is the second leading cause of death in India, and survivors often face years of rehabilitation. His openness about the realities of recovery — the daily medication, the dietary restrictions, the uncertainty about basic abilities — provides a rare public window into what millions of stroke survivors and their families navigate privately.
